papers.title: WITHDRAWN: A Modality-Invariant Measure of Neural Health
papers.abstract: Quantifying neural health with a single measure remains a major unmet challenge. Here, we report a physiological marker based on the spatial distribution of signal-derived energy correlates in the resting brain. We hypothesize that energy organization in the healthy brain approaches an entropy-maximizing, homeostatically regulated state characterized by five properties: lognormal energy distributions, balanced spatial allocation, statistical independence between regions, low energy variance, and temporal stability. Together, these properties define an energetic profile that the Neural Health Index (NHI) summarizes as a single score, computable from (scalp/intracranial) electroencephalography, magnetoencephalography, or functional magnetic resonance imaging. Across 808 participants spanning neurological, psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, and neurodegenerative disorders, NHI distinguished healthy from clinical populations with sensitivity and specificity exceeding 95% in internal and external validation, scaled with disease severity, tracked pharmacological treatment exposure, and generalized to unseen diagnoses. These findings support NHI as a disease-agnostic, modality-invariant candidate biomarker for disease stratification and treatment monitoring.

papers.title: Timing the Target: Exploring the Circadian Transcriptome of Biologic Therapies in Asthma.
papers.abstract: Background: Many of the immune pathways involved in asthma or in asthma treatment show circadian or diurnal variation. Understanding this variation can aid in biomarker discovery and/or therapy optimization. Objective: To evaluate if receptors, cytokines, and their pathways (n=46) targeted by currently approved biologics show significant diurnal rhythmicity and to identify their peak expression time. Methods: We used longitudinal bulk RNA sequencing datasets (discovery/replication cohorts: GSE113883 and GSE223613) and one microarray file (GSE39445) for cross-platform replication/validation. First, we used 16 canonical clock genes (including CLOCK, BMAL1, REV-ERB-beta) as positive controls to explore rhythmicity in each cohort. Thereafter, we evaluated if any targets of currently approved biologics or their corresponding receptors showed significant diurnal variation. For significant genes (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR<0.05), we estimated the baseline average, phase, peak-time of expression across the 24-hour day using clock time and quantified the cross-cohort consistency in the peak time of expression across the cohorts. Results: These cohorts included 453 longitudinal samples collected every two to four hours over a 24-28h cycle. Twelve (75%) of 16 evaluable clock genes showed significant rhythmicity. Only 34 of 46 (74%) asthma-related genes were evaluable across two or more cohorts. Of these 34 genes, 23 (68%) showed significant variation. Across all cohorts, the most preserved rhythmically expressed targets included many pathways or targets of monoclonal antibodies that are currently approved or in development: GATA3 and STAT6, master regulators of type 2 inflammation and IL4/IL13 signaling; chemokines, including the neutrophil chemoattractant, CXCL8; IL-5RA, benralizumab's target; FcRE1, suppressed by omalizumab; and IL1RL1(ST2) in clinical trials. Conclusion: Many therapeutic targets in asthma show significant diurnal rhythmicity. Future studies on how dosing time affects their therapeutic effectiveness while minimizing side effects are needed.

papers.title: Time of Day Dependent Effectiveness of Anti-IgE Therapy in Asthma: Clinical and Experimental Evidence
papers.abstract: BackgroundAsthma is a time-sensitive inflammatory disease whose activity exhibits daily (circadian) rhythms. An outstanding question is whether such temporal variations extend to advanced asthma treatments like biologics that are used for moderate-to-severe disease. ObjectiveTo examine how time-of-administration relates to the effectiveness of the anti-IgE biologic, omalizumab. MethodsWe performed a retrospective cohort study of omalizumab effectiveness in 153 patients with asthma with timestamped administration records. Time of day was modeled as a continuous variable and dichotomized into morning (8:00-11:59, n=74) versus afternoon (12:00-17:00, n=79) administration. Multivariable logistic regression and Cox time-to-event analyses were used to adjust for key covariates. For biological validation, we treated ovalbumin (OVA)-sensitized mice with anti-IgE antibody at various times of day and measured its impact on inflammatory lung pathology. ResultsReceiving the initial dose of omalizumab in the afternoon was associated with better response, defined as a 50% or more reduction in asthma exacerbations in the year after initiation (Odds ratio, OR: 5.20; 95% CI, 1.94-13.96). For each hour later in the day the initial dose of omalizumab was given, the odds of a response increased by 34% (adjusted OR, 1.34; 1.02-1.77). In OVA-sensitized mice, anti-IgE treatment attenuated inflammatory lung pathology, including OVA-induced airway hyperresponsiveness and type-2 inflammation-related gene expression, in a time-of-day-sensitive manner, with maximum effectiveness when dosed in the latter part of the dark phase, functionally analogous to the afternoon in humans. ConclusionThe timing of anti-IgE treatment for asthma may influence therapeutic success. These findings have implications for optimizing the effectiveness of respiratory biologics. Take-home messagesO_LIIgE-targeted therapy in patients with asthma and in murine experimental asthma varied in effectiveness based on administration time.
